newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-WOODRUFF, COSTA SCORE UPSETS AT ARIZONA MEN'S TOURNAMENT.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WOODRUFF, COSTA SCORE UPSETS AT ARIZONA MEN'S TOURNAMENT.

text.p: Chris Woodruff toppled third seed Carlos Moya, Jonas Bjorkman upset fourth seed Albert Costa and Mark Philippoussis boomed the hardest serve ever clocked on the ATP tour at the $328,000 Arizona men's tennis tournament Friday.

Woodruff defeated Moya 7-6 (10-8) 5-7 6-3 to earn a spot against Philippoussis in the semifinals Saturday. Bjorkman eliminated Costa 6-4 2-6 6-4 to set up a semifinal clash with eighth seed Richey Reneberg, a 6-4 6-2 winner over French qualifier Jerome Golmard.

Bjorkman's match had a bizarre ending. The Swede claimed victory while serving at 6-5, 40-0 following his eighth ace, and his Spanish opponent made an obscene gesture in frustration. That prompted chair umpire Norm Chryst to call a second code violation, ending the one hour, 35 minute match.
Costa said he was frustrated over his inability to hold serve. He lost serve five of 12 times, including the final three. "The match makes me crazy," he said.
Philippoussis set an all-time ATP Tour record with a 228.5 kph (142 mph ) rocket in his 7-5 6-3 victory over Byron Black of Zimbabwe.

"It felt extrememly smooth and effortless, said the 20-year-old Australian, who had 17 aces during the 73-minute sweep. "I just threw it up. I didn't try to hit it hard but my rhythm was so smooth, I didn't even feel like I hit the ball.
"I knew I was hitting big and I looked up and the crowd was pretty excited, so I knew it was big."

Philippoussis exploded his record-breaking bomb to go ahead 4-1 as Black just watched the ball whiz by. The fireball eclipsed the previous mark of 225 kph (139.8 mph) set by Britain's Greg Rusedski indoors at Beijing last year.
"I knew it was big but I didn't know it was that big," said Black. "I didn't even see it."
Woodruff admitted his two-hour, nine-minute baseline battle against Moya, the Australian Open finalist, was a dogfight until finally notching his third career victory over a Top 10 player.

"It takes a lot to beat a top player," said Woodruff, the world's 64th-ranked player after moving into his first semifinal of the year. "You can't just sit back there and let him dictate. You have to take your chances. I was just going for my shots under pressure."
Woodruff got the decisive break in the eight game to go ahead 5-3 when the Spaniard's inside-out forehand went long. He served out the match without any trouble.
"It's awfully tough to serve out a match against a top guy like that," said the American, who fired in 10 aces. "But you have to beat the top guys if you're going to do anything out here."
